name: Microsoft
summary: Microsoft senior engineering loops are commonly reported to weigh solid data-structures-and-algorithms coding heavily, usually written and talked through live, alongside system design for large-scale cloud services such as Azure workloads. Behavioural questions tend to be woven into most rounds instead of sitting in one dedicated interview, and they often probe growth mindset: how you learn from failure, work across teams and keep the customer in view.

loop.what: Commonly reported as a 45-60 minute call with one or two coding problems (arrays, strings, trees, hash maps) in a shared editor, sometimes with short questions about your background. Some teams use an online assessment instead.
tips: Clarify inputs and edge cases before coding
Talk through a brute-force approach, then optimise
Test your code by hand with a small example and an edge case

loop.what: Usually one or two rounds of medium (sometimes hard) DS&A problems: trees, graphs, linked lists, DP, string parsing. Interviewers are often reported to care about clean, working code and how you handle edge cases.
tips: Write production-quality code: clear names, null checks, helper functions
State time and space complexity without being asked
Expect follow-ups that change constraints (streaming input, memory limits)
Expect a short behavioural question at the start or end

loop.what: A design round for a cloud-scale service, for example storage, messaging, telemetry or configuration. Reported to focus on requirements, APIs, data partitioning, availability across regions and zones, and operational concerns.
tips: Pin down scale, SLAs and tenancy model early
Cover multi-region / availability-zone failure explicitly
Discuss safe deployment, monitoring and on-call operability
Name your trade-offs and when you would revisit them

loop.round: Object-oriented / low-level design or second design round
loop.what: Some loops are reported to include a class-design problem (parking lot, LRU cache, file system API) or a deeper dive into a past project's architecture.
tips: Start from use cases, then classes and responsibilities
Keep interfaces small and extensible
Be ready to defend design decisions from your own projects

loop.what: Questions about conflict, failure, learning, mentoring and customer impact, often asked in the first or last minutes of technical rounds rather than as a standalone interview.
tips: Prepare 6-8 STAR stories with measurable outcomes
Show what you learned and changed afterwards (growth mindset)
Highlight cross-team work and how you brought people along

loop.what: Widely reported as a final conversation with a senior leader or hiring manager, mixing technical depth, design and culture fit. Not every loop includes it, and accounts of its format vary.
tips: Expect broad questions about your judgement and career direction
Connect your experience to the team's product and customers
Have thoughtful questions ready about the team and its challenges

values.name: Growth mindset
values.meaning: Being a learn-it-all rather than a know-it-all: seeking feedback, learning from failure and staying curious.

values.name: Customer obsessed
values.meaning: Understanding customers' needs deeply and judging work by the difference it makes for them.

values.name: Diverse and inclusive
values.meaning: Seeking out different perspectives and making sure everyone can contribute fully.

values.name: One Microsoft
values.meaning: Working across team and organisational boundaries as one company towards shared goals.

values.name: Making a difference
values.meaning: Connecting your work to the mission of empowering every person and every organisation on the planet to achieve more.

valuesNote: These are paraphrases of Microsoft's publicly described culture (growth mindset plus customer obsessed, diverse and inclusive, One Microsoft, making a difference) and its stated mission. Exact official wording may differ and change over time; check Microsoft's careers and culture pages.
